title: Austin Accountant Arun Mago Gets 41 Months for COVID Loan Fraud and Money Laundering
excerpt: The 47-year-old certified public accountant fraudulently obtained nearly $1 million in PPP and EIDL loans, then laundered $150,000 he knew was cocaine money in an undercover operation. A judge ordered more than $900,000 in restitution and a $250,000 fine — and investigators noted his own book had a chapter claiming money laundering was untraceable.
body:
• Arun Mago, 47, an Austin-based certified public accountant, has been sentenced to 41 months in federal prison for money laundering and bank fraud involving COVID-19 relief loans.
  • Between April and November 2021 he obtained several fraudulent PPP and Economic Injury Disaster Loans for multiple business entities, totalling nearly $1 million, and used the money for real estate purchases.
  • Between October 2023 and July 2024 he laundered $150,000 in cash he knew to be proceeds of cocaine distribution — money supplied in an undercover operation.
  • US District Judge Robert Pitman also ordered more than $900,000 in restitution and a $250,000 fine.

An Austin accountant has been sentenced in federal court to 41 months in prison for money laundering and bank fraud that undermined the Paycheck Protection Program, the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas announced. Arun Mago, 47, was a certified public accountant running his own practice.

According to court documents, the case had two halves. During the pandemic, from about April 4 to November 23, 2021, Mago applied for and received several fraudulent PPP loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) for several business entities, totalling nearly $1 million. Bank records showed he transferred the funds into his personal account and used them for multiple real estate purchases.

Then, between October 2023 and July 2024 — years after the emergency programs closed — Mago laundered $150,000 in cash that he knew to be the proceeds of cocaine distribution. The money had been supplied through an undercover operation.

"Mago, who was a certified public accountant, wrote a book with a chapter titled 'Black Money' and claimed money laundering and tax evasion schemes were untraceable. I can only imagine his shock when we traced his more than $900,000 of COVID loan fraud and also got him on money laundering charges in an undercover operation."

— Christopher J. Altemus Jr., Special Agent in Charge, IRS Criminal Investigation, Texas Field Office

The Sentence

US District Judge Robert Pitman sentenced Mago to 41 months in prison and, in addition to the imprisonment, ordered him to pay over $900,000 in restitution and a $250,000 fine, the India Tribune reported. US Attorney Justin R. Simmons said Mago "not only defrauded the United States government during the chaotic COVID-19 pandemic but continued down his criminal path to launder a substantial amount of drug money."

https://x.com/AAGMcDonald/status/2115549984963870946

The case was investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation and the Office of the Texas Attorney General, and prosecuted by Assistant US Attorney Keith Henneke.

Why Pandemic Fraud Cases Are Still Landing

Mago's sentencing comes more than five years after the loans were issued. PPP and EIDL were designed for speed — lenders disbursed against borrower certifications with limited upfront verification — and investigators have been working through the backlog since, using bank records to trace where the money actually went. In Mago's case, the trail was unusually direct: loan funds moved into his personal account and into real estate, the pattern prosecutors look for first.

For diaspora professionals, the detail that will sting is the defendant's occupation. Mago was not a borrower who misunderstood a form; he was a CPA — the person clients pay to keep them compliant — who, prosecutors showed, ran the fraud himself and then wrote about untraceable money in print. Practising accountants convicted of fraud also face the loss of their licences, separate from the prison term.

What's Next

Mago begins a 41-month federal term, with restitution of more than $900,000 and the $250,000 fine payable under the court's schedule. The Justice Department's pandemic-fraud enforcement continues, and borrowers who took PPP or EIDL funds they were not entitled to remain exposed while investigations of 2020-21 loan files continue.
